## Welcome {#home}

### Malaria

**Learning Objectives:**

- Identify the agent, vector, and reservoir of malaria
- Describe the parasite life cycle in man and mosquito
- Distinguish the clinical types of malaria by species
- Recognize the WHO danger signs defining severe/complicated malaria
- Compare methods of diagnosis and outline treatment by species
- State the key malariometric indicators used in surveillance
- Describe India's malaria control programme (NVBDCP) and strategy

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
This module extends Chapter 6's general communicable-disease principles
(chain of infection, vector control) to malaria specifically — the
first of several vector-borne and enteric diseases covered as dedicated
modules.
:::

---

## Agent, Reservoir, and Vector {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Malaria is caused by four **Plasmodium** species, transmitted by the bite
of an infected **female Anopheles mosquito**:

| Species | Share of cases | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **P. vivax** | ~70% | Benign tertian; relapses (hypnozoites) |
| **P. falciparum** | ~25–30% | Malignant tertian; responsible for severe/fatal malaria; no relapse |
| **P. malariae** | uncommon | Quartan fever (every 4th day) |
| **P. ovale** | rare | Mainly Africa; relapses |

**Reservoir:** humans only — either a **case** (clinical malaria) or a
**carrier** (asymptomatic gametocyte carriage; children more often
carriers than adults).

---

## Life Cycle {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

The parasite completes its life cycle across **two hosts**:

- **In man (asexual cycle)** — sporozoites injected by the mosquito bite
  reach the liver, multiply into schizonts, and release merozoites into
  the blood. Merozoites invade RBCs (erythrocytic phase); rupture of
  infected RBCs causes the fever paroxysm. *P. vivax/ovale* leave dormant
  **hypnozoites** in the liver → later relapse; *P. falciparum* does not
  relapse.
- **In the mosquito (sexual cycle / sporogony)** — ingested gametocytes
  fertilize in the mosquito gut, forming an oocyst that produces
  sporozoites, which migrate to the salivary glands (10–20 days,
  temperature/humidity dependent) — the mosquito is now infective.

**Incubation period:** vivax ≈14 days · falciparum ≈12 days · malariae
≈28 days · ovale ≈17 days.

---

## Clinical Features {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

**Benign tertian (P. vivax):** the classic three-stage paroxysm — cold
stage (chills, rigors) → hot stage (103–104°F) → sweating stage — fever
on alternate days; repeated attacks → splenomegaly, anaemia.

**Malignant tertian (P. falciparum):** continuous fever, classic stages
often absent; can progress to **cerebral malaria** (convulsions, coma),
**blackwater fever** (haemoglobinuria), or **algid/septicaemic malaria**
(shock) — the life-threatening form.

**Quartan (P. malariae):** fever every 4th day. **Ovale malaria:** similar
to vivax, mainly in Africa.

---

## Severe Malaria: Recognizing Danger Signs {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Any of the following, in a patient with confirmed *P. falciparum*
infection, defines **severe/complicated malaria** requiring emergency
treatment — this is the structured version of the complications named
on the previous slide:

- **Cerebral malaria** — impaired consciousness or convulsions
- **Severe anaemia** — from massive RBC destruction
- **Renal failure** — including **blackwater fever** (massive
  haemoglobinuria)
- **Pulmonary oedema / ARDS**
- **Hypoglycaemia** — worsened by quinine treatment itself
- **Circulatory collapse/shock** — algid/septicaemic malaria
- **Metabolic (lactic) acidosis**

**Why this list matters clinically:** severe malaria requires
**parenteral** antimalarial therapy (IV artesunate, the WHO-preferred
agent) rather than the oral regimens used for uncomplicated malaria —
recognizing any one of these signs changes the treatment route
immediately.

---

## Diagnosis {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

All suspected cases require **parasitological confirmation**:

- **Light microscopy** — thick smear (detects presence/absence); thin
  smear (identifies species and parasite stage) — remains the gold
  standard
- **Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs)** — immunochromatographic antigen
  detection, results in ~15 minutes; can distinguish *P. falciparum* from
  non-falciparum

**Suspected case definition:** fever in a person living in or having
recently visited an endemic area during transmission season, with no
other confirmed diagnosis.

---

## Treatment Principles {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

- **P. vivax** — chloroquine (blood stages) **plus** primaquine for 14
  days (clears liver hypnozoites, prevents relapse)
- **P. falciparum** — Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (**ACT**,
  e.g. artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) plus a single dose of
  primaquine (gametocytocidal, blocks transmission)
- **Primaquine is contraindicated** in pregnancy, infants, and G6PD
  deficiency (risk of haemolysis)
- **Mixed infections** involving falciparum are treated as falciparum
  malaria
- **Pregnancy:** ACT in the 2nd/3rd trimester for falciparum (quinine in
  the 1st trimester); chloroquine for vivax

---

## Malariometric Indicators {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

Used to measure transmission intensity and evaluate control programmes:

- **Annual Parasite Incidence (API)** — confirmed cases per 1,000
  population per year (India's key programme metric)
- **Slide Positivity Rate (SPR)** / **Slide Falciparum Rate (SFR)** —
  % of examined blood smears positive overall / positive for falciparum
- **Infant Parasite Rate** — most sensitive indicator of active
  transmission; considered interrupted if zero for 3 consecutive years
- **Entomological indices** — vector density, human blood index,
  sporozoite rate (vector-side transmission risk)

---

## NVBDCP and Malaria Elimination {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

India's malaria programme has evolved considerably:

`NMCP (1953) → NMEP (1958) → Modified Plan of Operation (1977) → National Anti-Malaria Programme (1999) → NVBDCP (2003–04) → National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016–2030`

**Control strategy (three-pronged):** early diagnosis and complete
treatment (passive + active surveillance) · integrated vector control
(indoor residual spray, ITNs/LLINs, source reduction) · behaviour change
communication and community participation.

**Vaccine:** RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix®) — WHO-recommended since October
2021, the first licensed anti-parasite vaccine; effective against
*P. falciparum* only, ~40% efficacy, 4-dose schedule from 5 months of
age.

**India's progress:** Annual Parasite Incidence fell from 2.09 (2000) to
0.13 (2022); malaria deaths fell from 932 to 83 over the same period.

### Question 1

Which Plasmodium species is responsible for the large majority of
severe, life-threatening malaria?

- P. vivax
- [P. falciparum]{.correct data-explanation="P. falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria and is responsible for nearly all severe and fatal malaria, including cerebral malaria."}
- P. malariae
- P. ovale
:::

## Self-Check: Question 2 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 2

Primaquine is given in P. vivax malaria primarily to:

- Kill blood-stage parasites and end the fever paroxysm
- [Clear liver hypnozoites and prevent relapse]{.correct data-explanation="Chloroquine acts on blood stages; primaquine is the only drug that clears dormant liver hypnozoites in P. vivax/ovale, preventing relapse."}
- Provide immediate symptomatic relief
- Sterilize the Anopheles vector
:::

## Self-Check: Question 3 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

### Question 3

Which malariometric indicator is considered the most sensitive marker of
active malaria transmission in a community?

- Slide Positivity Rate
- Child Spleen Rate
- [Infant Parasite Rate]{.correct data-explanation="Infants have had the shortest possible exposure window, so a positive infant parasite rate indicates recent, active transmission; it is considered interrupted only if zero for 3 consecutive years."}
- Annual Blood Examination Rate

## Self-Check: Question 4 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 4

A patient with confirmed P. falciparum malaria develops impaired
consciousness. This finding means the patient:

- Has uncomplicated malaria and can continue oral treatment
- [Has severe/complicated malaria and requires parenteral treatment such as IV artesunate]{.correct data-explanation="Impaired consciousness (a feature of cerebral malaria) is one of the WHO danger signs defining severe malaria, which requires parenteral therapy rather than the oral regimens used for uncomplicated malaria."}
- Should be given oral primaquine immediately
- Only needs a repeat RDT to confirm
:::
